title: The palette and getting around
summary: Every command by name, any file by a few letters, any symbol, definition or reference in one key, and workspace settings the whole team shares.

steps.title: One shortcut to find all the others
body: VS Code has hundreds of commands and you will remember a dozen keys. The **command palette** finds the rest by name:
| Quick Open a file by name | `Ctrl+P` | `Cmd+P` |
| Go to symbol in this file | `Ctrl+Shift+O` | `Cmd+Shift+O` |
| Go to symbol in the workspace | `Ctrl+T` | `Cmd+T` |
Quick Open is fuzzy: `ordsvc` finds `OrderService.cs`. Its box also takes prefixes: `>` turns it into the palette, `:42` goes to line 42, `@` lists symbols, `#` searches workspace symbols.
Why it matters: reaching for the mouse and the file tree costs seconds a hundred times a day. The palette also shows each command's shortcut next to its name, which is how you learn new ones.

steps.prompt: Match the shortcut (Windows / Linux) to what it does.
pairs: open a file by typing part of its name
jump to a function or class in this file
search the text of every file

steps.prompt: A stack trace says `src/billing/InvoiceService.cs:214`. What is the fastest way there in VS Code?
options: Open the Explorer, expand `src`, then `billing`, and scroll
`Ctrl+G` and type `214`, in whatever file is open
steps.explain: Quick Open matches the file fuzzily and `:214` jumps to the line in the same step. `Ctrl+G` only moves within the file that is already open.

steps.title: Code navigation through the language server
body: With a language extension installed (C# Dev Kit, Python, TypeScript is built in), VS Code understands the code, not just the text:
**Rename symbol (`F2`)** changes the declaration and every real use across files, and skips the same word in strings and comments. A text replace cannot tell those apart.

steps.prompt: Rename symbol (`F2`) or search and replace (`Ctrl+Shift+H`)?
items: Rename a C# method called from 30 files
Rename a property whose name is also a common word in comments
Fix a misspelled word across the Markdown docs
Rename a TypeScript interface used across packages

steps.title: Settings: user, workspace, language
body: VS Code settings are JSON files, layered. Later layers win:

2. **User** settings, for you on every project: `%APPDATA%\Code\User\settings.json` on Windows, `~/Library/Application Support/Code/User/settings.json` on macOS, `~/.config/Code/User/settings.json` on Linux.
3. **Workspace** settings, committed with the repo so the whole team gets them: `.vscode/settings.json`.
Inside either file, a `"[python]": { ... }` block overrides settings for one language only.

`Ctrl+,` (`Cmd+,`) opens the settings UI; the palette command **Preferences: Open Workspace Settings (JSON)** opens the file. The files are **JSONC**: VS Code allows `//` comments and trailing commas in them.

steps.prompt: Your user settings say `"editor.tabSize": 2`. The repo's `.vscode/settings.json` says `"[python]": { "editor.tabSize": 4 }`. What tab size do you get in a Python file of that repo, and in its YAML files?
options: 2 in both: user settings always win
4 in both: workspace settings replace all user settings
Whatever the file had last time it was saved
steps.explain: Workspace settings override user settings key by key, and a language block applies only to that language. Everything the workspace does not set keeps your user value.

steps.title: Workspace settings for the team
prompt: Give everyone who opens `~/shop` the same basics. Create `~/shop/.vscode/settings.json` with:
- `files.eol`: `"\n"` (LF line endings, so shell scripts work on Linux)
Then commit it (`git add .vscode/settings.json`, `git commit -m ...`), because a workspace setting nobody else has does not help the team.
The checks read the file with `jq`, which needs plain JSON: leave out comments and trailing commas here, even though VS Code itself accepts them. `jq . file` is your syntax check.

checks.name: settings.json is valid JSON
checks.fail: `~/shop/.vscode/settings.json` is missing or not valid JSON. `jq . ~/shop/.vscode/settings.json` shows the error.

checks.name: format on save, LF, final newline, trim
checks.cmd: jq -e '."editor.formatOnSave" == true and ."files.eol" == "\n" and ."files.insertFinalNewline" == true and ."files.trimTrailingWhitespace" == true' ~/shop/.vscode/settings.json
checks.fail: One of the four top-level settings is missing or has the wrong value. Keys with dots go in quotes: `"editor.formatOnSave": true`.

checks.name: the settings are committed
checks.fail: Commit `.vscode/settings.json` so the team gets it (and leave no uncommitted changes to it).

hints: In JSON, `\n` inside a string is the newline character: `"files.eol": "\n"`. Check the file with `jq . ~/shop/.vscode/settings.json`.
`cd ~/shop && git add .vscode/settings.json && git commit -m "Share editor settings"`.
steps.explain: Commit settings that affect the code (formatting, line endings, tab size), not personal taste (themes, font size). `files.eol` only applies to new files; for line endings across tools and editors, a `.gitattributes` with `* text=auto eol=lf` is the stronger fix, and `.editorconfig` shares indent rules with editors other than VS Code.
